source.title: The Price of Implicit Bias in Adversarially Robust Generalization
source.authors: Nikolaos Tsilivis; N. Frank; Nathan Srebro; Julia Kempe

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; some equations, figures and table layouts are flattened in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests how optimizer and architecture change robust generalization under adversarial training. Its results qualify the catalog claim: optimizer effects reverse across model families and can change sharply with perturbation magnitude and data regime. Robust generalization is the measured target, so this is a challenge/refinement rather than a direct test of ordinary generalization.
record.gate_note: The study tests robust ERM and robust train/test gaps, rather than the ordinary natural-label generalization claim in most versions. Rows capture its own experiments that vary optimizer, architecture, training perturbation, data regime, and evaluation regime. Theoretical bounds and cited findings are not rows. Figure-only result values are retained as figure-only; no precise values were reconstructed from plots.
record.test_reason: The study tests implicit optimization bias in adversarially robust generalization, but none of V1–V8. Its clean-evaluation controls also lack the required interventions: sign descent is not an adaptive optimizer comparison, and CNNs and fully connected networks are not compared on a matched classification task. These results do not justify T5 for the stated versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate: the authors identify implicit optimization bias as a contributing factor to robust generalization gaps and recommend exploring first-order algorithms beyond GD. The proposed connection to robust overfitting is tentative, based on contrasting GD and SD training curves, rather than an established causal explanation.
record.recipe_differences: The study focuses on adversarially robust empirical risk minimization and robust train/test performance, while the claim versions concern ordinary generalization, memorization, and other specific interventions. The paper includes theoretical analysis and synthetic and MNIST experiments under ℓ∞ perturbations.
record.method_sensitivity: Robust generalization changes with optimizer, architecture, perturbation magnitude, training-set size, teacher/data sparsity, and whether evaluation is robust or clean. In the CNN setting, the direction of the GD versus SD advantage differs from the fully connected homogeneous setting. SD is unstable near convergence in one large-sample, zero-perturbation condition.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic linear classification, robust generalization depends on optimizer geometry, parameterization, sparsity, and perturbation magnitude. The dense/dense setting has similar clean ERM generalization across algorithms but robust performance differences exceeding 20 percentage points with few samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Implicit optimization bias can substantially affect adversarially robust generalization, with its benefit depending on the data and threat model.

fits_no_version.finding: For fully connected MNIST 2-versus-7 networks at epsilon = 0.2, SD exceeds GD robust test accuracy by 4.11 percentage points over three seeds despite both reaching 100% robust training accuracy. For multiclass MNIST CNNs, GD performs better than SD, especially with fewer samples and larger perturbations. The architecture experiments use different classification tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative robust generalization of GD and sign descent can differ across tested architecture-and-task settings.

fits_no_version.finding: For dense/dense synthetic data after robust training, GD can generalize better on clean inputs while CD generalizes better under adversarial perturbations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choices that improve robust generalization can worsen clean generalization.

record.problems: Most plotted experimental results have no extractable numeric values in the supplied flattened figures. Neural-network experiments use three random seeds. The CNN comparison uses different constant learning rates for GD and SD; the authors report SD diverged at larger learning rates tried. Robust evaluation for neural networks uses 10 PGD iterations. The main generalization results concern robust ERM and do not directly establish ordinary generalization claims in the mapped versions.
record.rows_left_out: No separately recoverable per-point rows for the linear-model curves in Figures 1, 2, 5, or 6, or the CNN performance-gap curve in Figure 3 (right): extracted figures contain curves or heatmaps without recoverable values. Appendix E Figure 8 has multiple separate dataset-size and perturbation conditions; the recoverable table records the plotted conditions described in the supplied text, but omits additional unlisted figure cells due to the 60-row limit and the inability to assign exact plotted values. The paper's theoretical statements and cited prior-work results are not experimental result rows.

untested.parts: Matched random-label memorization and natural-label held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum, limited versus broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Batch-size interventions under fixed epoch budgets and compensating training recipes.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and removing dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps against other measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain unlinked to V1–V8. Their cannot_determine states concern applicability to these versions, not whether the study establishes its own robust-generalization findings. Input perturbation robustness is distinct from the weight perturbation sharpness in V7.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and ordinary generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and ordinary test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons for ordinary image generalization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum under ordinary image or language benchmarks.
Batch-size effects at fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measured properties tracking an ordinary train/test generalization gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring ordinary test accuracy.
